Escalation Analysis Briefing

Purpose
This file consolidates the key quantitative results for the escalation-analysis section so they can be fed directly into another AI model for drafting thesis text.

Data Sources
- Architecture B final results: results/Final_Architecture_B_results.csv
- Architecture A final results: results/Final_Architecture_A_results.csv
- Generated analysis folder: results/escalation_analysis

Method Summary
- Architecture A step 1-4 analysis uses the full 1,189-question file: results/Final_Architecture_A_results.csv
- For Architecture A step 1, each question is labeled Unanimous if all three base models agree, otherwise Split if the vote is 2-1.
- For Architecture A step 2, average the three model confidence scores per question and split into High vs. Low using the median average confidence across all 1,189 questions.
- For Architecture A step 4, the exact requested composite score is used:
  composite_score = (1 if unanimous else 0) + average_confidence
- Architecture A questions are sorted in descending order by this composite score to build the coverage-accuracy curve.
- Architecture B agreement-status and confidence analyses use the final round of deliberation.
- For Architecture B confidence bins, average the three models' round-2 confidence scores per question, then split questions into high vs. low confidence using a median split.
- The Architecture B coverage-accuracy curve sorts questions by signal strength:
  1. unanimous final-round votes first
  2. then descending average round-2 confidence
- The Architecture A coverage-accuracy curve uses an analogous ranking:
  1. unanimous base-model votes first
  2. then descending average model confidence
- The Architecture A vs. B comparison uses the full 1,189-question final result files for both systems.

Architecture A: Step 1, Accuracy by Agreement Status
- Total questions: 1,189
- Median average confidence threshold for step 2: 0.9100
- Unanimous questions: n = 978, accuracy = 88.34%
- Split questions: n = 211, accuracy = 57.82%

Interpretation
- Agreement status is a very strong reliability signal in Architecture A.
- Unanimous cases are dramatically more accurate than split cases.

Architecture A: Step 2, Accuracy by Average Confidence
- High-confidence questions: n = 609, accuracy = 94.75%
- Low-confidence questions: n = 580, accuracy = 70.52%

Interpretation
- Average confidence is also a strong discriminator for Architecture A.
- High-confidence cases are substantially more accurate than low-confidence cases.

Architecture A: Step 3, Combined 2x2 Table
- Unanimous + high confidence: n = 563, accuracy = 97.87%
- Unanimous + low confidence: n = 415, accuracy = 75.42%
- Split + high confidence: n = 46, accuracy = 56.52%
- Split + low confidence: n = 165, accuracy = 58.18%

Interpretation
- The highest-quality Architecture A bucket is unanimous + high confidence, reaching 97.87% accuracy.
- Nearly all of the highly reliable cases are concentrated in that cell.
- Split cases remain weak even when average confidence is relatively high, which suggests agreement is the more important escalation signal.

Architecture A: Step 4, Coverage-Accuracy Curve
- Composite score definition:
  composite_score = (1 if unanimous else 0) + average_confidence
- Coverage-accuracy checkpoints:
  - Top 10% auto-resolved: n = 118, accuracy = 100.00%
  - Top 20% auto-resolved: n = 237, accuracy = 99.58%
  - Top 25% auto-resolved: n = 297, accuracy = 99.66%
  - Top 50% auto-resolved: n = 594, accuracy = 97.47%
  - Top 75% auto-resolved: n = 891, accuracy = 90.12%
  - Top 100% auto-resolved: n = 1,189, accuracy = 82.93%

Interpretation
- Architecture A supports a very strong selective-automation policy.
- Using the exact composite ranking, the highest-signal half of cases achieves 97.47% accuracy.
- This provides a strong basis for recommending Architecture A with escalation on low-score cases.

Architecture B: Agreement Status Accuracy
- Total questions: 1,189
- Unanimous 3-0 questions: n = 1,052, accuracy = 78.99%
- Split 2-1 questions: n = 137, accuracy = 54.01%

Interpretation
- Final-round unanimity is a strong signal of reliability in Architecture B.
- Split decisions are much less reliable than unanimous ones.

Architecture B: Confidence Bin Accuracy
- Confidence split method: median split on average round-2 confidence
- Median average confidence threshold: 0.8067
- High-confidence questions: n = 600, accuracy = 85.83%
- Low-confidence questions: n = 589, accuracy = 66.21%

Interpretation
- Average confidence meaningfully separates easier vs. harder Architecture B cases.
- High-confidence cases are substantially more accurate than low-confidence cases.

Architecture B: 2x2 Table Combining Agreement and Confidence
- Unanimous + high confidence: n = 522, accuracy = 89.85%
- Unanimous + low confidence: n = 530, accuracy = 68.30%
- Split + high confidence: n = 78, accuracy = 58.97%
- Split + low confidence: n = 59, accuracy = 47.46%

Interpretation
- The strongest Architecture B auto-resolution bucket is unanimous + high confidence.
- The weakest bucket is split + low confidence.
- This supports an escalation policy where low-signal cases are routed to human review instead of auto-resolved.

Architecture B: Coverage-Accuracy Curve Checkpoints
- Top 10% auto-resolved: n = 118, accuracy = 100.00%
- Top 20% auto-resolved: n = 237, accuracy = 99.16%
- Top 25% auto-resolved: n = 297, accuracy = 97.64%
- Top 50% auto-resolved: n = 594, accuracy = 87.04%
- Top 75% auto-resolved: n = 891, accuracy = 80.58%
- Top 100% auto-resolved: n = 1,189, accuracy = 76.11%

Interpretation
- Architecture B can achieve very high accuracy on its strongest-signal subset.
- Accuracy declines as coverage expands, which is the standard pattern expected in selective-prediction or escalation settings.
- This curve supports the argument that signal-aware escalation can improve deployed reliability relative to resolving every case automatically.

Architecture A vs. B Coverage-Accuracy Comparison
- Comparison figure: results/escalation_analysis/coverage_accuracy_comparison.png
- Architecture A overall accuracy: 82.93%
- Architecture B overall accuracy: 76.11%
- Prefixes where Architecture A has higher cumulative accuracy: 980
- Prefixes where Architecture B has higher cumulative accuracy: 127
- Tied prefixes: 82

Checkpoint Comparison
- Top 10% auto-resolved: A = 99.15%, B = 100.00%, gap = -0.85 percentage points
- Top 20% auto-resolved: A = 99.58%, B = 99.16%, gap = +0.42 percentage points
- Top 25% auto-resolved: A = 99.66%, B = 97.64%, gap = +2.02 percentage points
- Top 50% auto-resolved: A = 97.47%, B = 87.04%, gap = +10.44 percentage points
- Top 75% auto-resolved: A = 90.24%, B = 80.58%, gap = +9.65 percentage points
- Top 100% auto-resolved: A = 82.93%, B = 76.11%, gap = +6.81 percentage points

Interpretation
- Architecture A is the better-performing deployment candidate overall.
- Architecture A is better than Architecture B across most coverage thresholds, especially at moderate and high coverage.
- Architecture A does not strictly dominate Architecture B at every single prefix, because Architecture B is slightly better at the very top 10% slice.
- The defensible claim is therefore:
  Architecture A yields higher overall accuracy and better coverage-accuracy tradeoffs across most of the operating range, which supports recommending independent aggregation over deliberative debate for deployment.

Suggested Thesis Framing
- The escalation analysis shows that model agreement and confidence provide usable signals for selective automation.
- In Architecture A specifically, agreement and confidence separate high-reliability and low-reliability cases very sharply.
- Within Architecture B, unanimous and high-confidence cases are substantially more reliable than split and low-confidence cases.
- However, when comparing deployment-oriented coverage-accuracy curves, Architecture A remains the stronger system overall and across most practical coverage thresholds.
- Therefore, even if Architecture B admits a useful escalation policy, the stronger recommendation is to deploy Architecture A with selective escalation rather than Architecture B.
